To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social capital is a complex and multidimensional phenomenon that is context dependent.
the use of mixed methods is a practical and useful way to assess the nature and extent social capital in low-income communities.

(1) Social capital is a multidimensional phenomenon that can be usefully assessed in low income countries; (2) Mixed methods can provide a richer and more comprehensive picture of the social capital landscape in poor communities; and (3) The use of mixed methods can be greatly improved through careful attention to issues of sampling, data collection and analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to assess social capital and the extent to which social capital is a useful concept in the context of low income communities.
how social capital can best be measured, and how such measurement can be used to inform development policy and practice.
the following questions: How do social relations in poor countries differ from those of the rich?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

social capital is an elusive and complex phenomenon, which cannot be captured by a single measure or method, but rather is best understood by drawing on multiple methods to capture its various manifestations.

social capital assessment is not a ‘one-size fits all’ exercise, and that researchers need to be flexible in their approaches, and open to the possibilities of new methods and new ways of thinking about the nature of social capital in the context of the communities and countries that they are researching.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social capital is a complex and multidimensional construct, and as such, it is not possible to measure it in any single way.
social capital is a useful concept that has the potential to help us understand the nature and extent, and also the limitations, of social relationships and networks in poor communities.
the use of both qualitative and quantitative techniques is necessary for a full assessment of social capital.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social capital is not an all-or-nothing affair.

, despite the many challenges involved in measuring social capital, it is possible to do so in low income settings, and that the benefits of doing so can be substantial, particularly in terms of improving our ability to understand how and why certain development interventions succeed or fail.

social capital assessment is best undertaken using a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods, with each approach complementing the other in a way that allows for a more complete picture to be painted.
